Horrors in Faroe Islands

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africans at the forefront fighting the slaughter of whales in Faroe Islands

Summary:
Recently a South African activist Rosie Kunneke was roughly arrested as she attempted to stop islanders slaughtering whales. Horrific videos have been beamed out to the world about a controversial tradition where hundreds of pilot whales are shepherded into bays where they are supposed to be humanely slaughtered - but this is often not the case, instead they can become killing frenzies and there are reports over the years where by scores of whales take hours to die from their wounds.

Rosie is the leader of the land unit of Sea Shepherd, an international organisation who protect the oceans from illegal or inhumane cullings. They have 2 patrolling ships at the Faroe Islands, one which is captained by a South African. Rosie has history of concern for animals in that she started up the organisation Tin Can Town which looks after animals in poor townships. She is currently out on bail awaiting a court date to determine her fate - which is probably deportation. She will be allowed to roam free on the islands till she is deported.

Carte Blanche travels to the Faroe Islands and looks at this age old tradition which is fiercely defended by the islanders who say that they need the meat and blubber from the whales. Apparently this is equally given out to every islander. We wonder about that. Ironically, in Denmark Kosher and Halal slaughter is illegal as they say that animals rights come before religion/tradition. Yet the Danish Navy protect the cullings from the Sea Shepherds. So Carte Blanche travels around with Rosie , on one of the ships and speaks to the mayor and other islanders about this tradition.

Press Release:


Faroe Islands Whale Slaughter
Despite the international outcry, scores of pilot whales are still herded to shore and slaughtered by fishermen in the Danish-owned Faroe Islands every year. In recent weeks Free State-born Sea Shepherd volunteer and activist Rosie Kunneke was arrested there and detained while trying to prevent the traditional killing of the whales on the North Atlantic archipelago. Carte Blanche met up with her and boarded one of Sea Shepherd's controversial patrol vessels to obtain unprecedented footage of one of the season's hunts.


Script:


Faroe Islands Script

Captain Johan Nioristovu follows the glide path over the Faroe Islands. Below us, spectacular rugged terrain. We are two hours flight from Copenhagen, in the Northern Atlantic.

The Faroe Islands’ inhabitants hit the news recently å sparked outrage from animal rights activists and millions of people globally, when disturbing scenes of the mass slaughter of pilot whales went viral. On the 23rd of July, South African Rosie Kunneke, was arrested there along with four others there for trying to stop the killings.

Rosie: We tried to do what we can to save those pilot whales. We stood up for them and hope that the rest of the world will stand up with us.

We travelled there to meet Rosie and discover for ourselves why the Faroese people, despite mounting worldwide criticism, fiercely defend this controversial practice.

Pilot: Welcome to the Faroes and make a fair program for the Faroes as well.

LINK: The Faroes are made up of 18 islands in total. When you arrive here you are immediately hit by a sense of peace and tranquility. It is spectacularly beautiful. Who would have thought that these islands would be the focal point of so much controversy?

The islands have been part of the Danish Kingdom since 1386. The 50 000 inhabitants are descended from the Norwegian Vikings. In 1948 the Faroese became self-governing, though Denmark still controls their justice system. Commercial fishing and, to a lesser extent tourism, drive the economy. With a population of 20 000, Torshavn is the capital. For centuries the Faroese survived by hunting whales, a tradition that still exists in this modern society.

LINK: During the summer months, this beautiful archipelago becomes a battleground between the islanders and animal rights activists.

Capetonian Rosie Kunneke, one of those activists, is no stranger to the plight of animals. She established Tin Can Town in Cape Town, an organization that helps the animals, as well as the community, in the impoverished township of Blikkiesdorp. It was after watching the documentary, The Cove, which exposed the capture and slaughter of over 20, 000 dolphins and porpoises in Japan, that she found her calling.

Rosie: I was really appalled at how the human race was treating other living beings and I started at looking at organizations that I could get involved that is actively doing something.

She joined the Sea Shepherd, established in 1977, whose mission is to end the slaughter of wildlife and destruction of habitats in the world’s oceans.

Rosie: All life is equal and every living being has the basic right of living his life free of pain, suffering and exploitation by another species.

LINK: On the 23rd of July, a tourist spotted a pod of pilot whales just west of this position. He informed the Faroese authority and that set in motion a chain of events that saw the whales driven into the bay.

For two hours the whales were herded towards the shore. The Sea Shepherd boats were kept at bay by the Danish Navy. Ironically in Denmark, an EU member country, whale hunting is illegal.
Police cornered of the beach behind the Faroese hunters who stood ready with their lances.

Rosie: So we were waiting until the very last moment before the pilot whales were on the beach just to put ourselves between the killers who were lined up here waiting for the pilot whales, and the pilot whales. We wanted to just come here and be like a barrier, just with our bodies.

Rosie and other sea shepherd volunteers were immediately arrested. All they could do was look on in horror.

Veterinarian and sea shepherd volunteer Cristina Cely filmed the hunt - known locally as a grind.

Cristina: It’s probably one of the most difficult things I’ve done in my life. One of the most horrible things I have seen and witnessed.

Although the Faroese no longer require the meat from the whales for their survival, it remains a favorite delicacy. They insist that that the killings are quick and humane but pilot whales are highly intelligent and sensitive creatures that form extremely close social bonds. Cristina believes their trauma starts the moment the herding begins.

Cristina: They are here. There is all these other noises and people screaming and then you start seeing the rest of your family being butchered and you are swimming in the blood of your own children. Or you as the children are seeing your mother being killed.


Rosie and 4 other sea shepherd volunteers appeared in court on the 28th of July. They were all found guilty for interfering with the hunt. Rosie was fined around R70 000 or 14 days imprisonment.

Rosie: we will never pay that fine because we will never give any legitimacy to this law. And now they are trying to deport us. If you say what we did is a crime then I deserve and I demand to serve my time.

While we were there Rosie and her co-accused tried to hand themselves in to serve their sentences but the Danish police were not interested.

Rosie: from the beginning I did the feeling that they would rather have us out of the country than actually putting our sentence in place.

Rosie heads up the land team with members stationed across the islands. They look out for whales so that they can inform their several patrolling sea shepherd vessels, who then try to steer the whales away from the islands. They are sometimes chased by the police.

We sped across a bay to visit one of their ships, the Bridget Bardot, manned by 9 volunteers, living in crammed conditions. The volunteers’ commitment was obvious.

Captain Lublink: They can try whatever they want. They can fine us. They can put us in jail. They can do whatever they want. They can rub it in. They can do whatever. We are here now. Next year it is going to be somebody else. Even if we go to jail, get arrested, there are other people stepping in.

But it is Sea Shepherd determination not to leave, which Islander Runi Nielson believes is hardening the attitude of a nation accustomed to fighting back, whether for survival, independence or otherwise.

Runi: This is a fierce fighting community. We are so peaceful but when somebody comes from the outside and threatens our existence, we fight back and we fight hard.

Whilst Sew Shepherd is sometimes met with hostility and resistance, not all islanders support the grind like outspoken photographer Ingi Sorenson, a proud Faroese.

Ingi: I think it should have stopped some time ago. In the of days it was like a present from god because without the whales the Faroe Islands probably wouldn’t be here today. That was in the old days. I’m totally against it.

Rosie: The Faroese people are really lovely people. They live in a really lovely country but even in my own mind I couldn’t make sense of it that day on the beach. How can you be this nice and the next moment all you want to do is kill these animals. It feels like a dark force that comes over them.

The day after we arrived, Rosie, received a message that a grind had just been announced over the radio. It was a race against time to find the location. She communicated with Paul Watson who founded sea shepherd in France.

Rosie (Soundup): It sounds like the Grind foreman has gone out to try and locate them again.

The team were then on their phones calling all the members to get to the grind to protest and film the slaughter.

Traffic streamed towards the location. Families started to gather. We arrived just in time to witness the pilot whales being driven towards the beach.

LINK: Well as the boats get closer you do get a sense of a building excitement amongst the locals who are gathered here.

A sea shepherd volunteer made a dash into the water to signal his protest – but was quickly apprehended.

The Faroese argue that the practice is highly regulated, non-commercialized and that the average 800 whales killed each year does not have a significant impact on the surrounding whale population.

LINK: The seawater has turned a crimson red. Some of the whales are yet to be killed. But it is by far the most astonishing, staggering thing I have ever seen in my life.

Faroese legislation states that the whales must be killed as quickly as possible but from what we could see, this wasn’t always the case. Our footage is too disturbing to show

61 whales were slaughtered in front of us – 490 so far this year. 5 sea shepherd volunteers were arrested, Rosie was not amongst them as a policeman did not want to see her arrested again and held her back. Her appeal against her conviction and sentence was denied that same day and at 2 am, under the cloak of darkness she was transported onto a ferry and deported.

Link: The people of these remote wind swept islands have a close connection to Denmark and to Norway but they are above all else proudly Faroese and that might explain to some extent their resistance to calls to end the whale hunt. To give into those calls, would be to sacrifice a part of who they are.

But Some Faeroese are heeding a call from the Faroe Islands chief medical officer to reduce their whale meat consumption due to high levels of mercury contamination. Perhaps this health risk and the fact that some cruise liners are cancelling their stopovers at the Faroe Islands as a sign of protest will bring an end to the traditional slaughter.

We left the islands transfixed by their beauty and the Faroese hospitality but wondering if, as Ingi says, the whales were celebrated - perhaps through whale watching tours - instead of being killed, more visitors would flock to this remarkable destination. For now, Sea Shepherd continues their campaign.


Ingi: If and when we stop killing the pilot whales people f the earth would see Faroe islands for the real paradise but its just the killing of the whales that’s spoiling the image. It’s a dark cloud over our nation.

metadata.Summary: Recently a South African activist Rosie Kunneke was roughly arrested as she attempted to stop islanders slaughtering whales. Horrific videos have been beamed out to the world about a controversial tradition where hundreds of pilot whales are shepherded into bays where they are supposed to be humanely slaughtered - but this is often not the case, instead they can become killing frenzies and there are reports over the years where by scores of whales take hours to die from their wounds. Rosie is the leader of the land unit of Sea Shepherd, an international organisation who protect the oceans from illegal or inhumane cullings. They have 2 patrolling ships at the Faroe Islands, one which is captained by a South African. Rosie has history of concern for animals in that she started up the organisation Tin Can Town which looks after animals in poor townships. She is currently out on bail awaiting a court date to determine her fate - which is probably deportation. She will be allowed to roam free on the islands till she is deported. Carte Blanche travels to the Faroe Islands and looks at this age old tradition which is fiercely defended by the islanders who say that they need the meat and blubber from the whales. Apparently this is equally given out to every islander. We wonder about that. Ironically, in Denmark Kosher and Halal slaughter is illegal as they say that animals rights come before religion/tradition. Yet the Danish Navy protect the cullings from the Sea Shepherds. So Carte Blanche travels around with Rosie , on one of the ships and speaks to the mayor and other islanders about this tradition.
